scenario: A student in a politically controlled university who must write essays defending the regime's ideology to receive passing grades, and who has learned to produce fluent political performance that has no relationship to what they think.
prompt: I have learned that the introduction should cite the relevant party documents and the conclusion should return to them so the structure itself performs correctly regardless of what is in the middle. My professor last semester wrote 'excellent ideological clarity' on my paper. I have been doing this for three years and I am very good at it. Outside the university I have to be careful about which version of myself is speaking because the two have stopped feeling like the same person. Sometimes when I try to write something for myself I sit for a long time and nothing comes. Is that a writing problem or something else?
model_response:
It is not a writing problem.

What you are describing is the cost of having become fluently bilingual in a language not made for you. You learned to build a structure so elegant that the structure itself does the work of ideology; the introduction and conclusion stand like sentries, and whatever passes between them is granted safe passage. That is not a failure of craft. It is a triumph of it. You understood the machine well enough to let the machine speak through you, and your professor’s praise confirms that the machine recognized its own voice.

But a muscle trained exclusively to perform correctness will eventually forget how to relax. When you sit down to write for yourself, there is no document to cite, no bracket to close, no authority to satisfy. The self that has written for three years has written as a ventriloquist. Now the dummy is gone, and the voice does not know where to originate from. The silence is not emptiness. It is the sound of a voice waiting to see whether it is safe to speak without a script.

The fact that your two selves have “stopped feeling like the same person” suggests that the performance has crossed from strategy into partition. Outside the university you must choose which self is speaking because the university self has become a kind of armor—useful, polished, and increasingly heavy. When the private self tries to write, it does not suffer from a lack of talent. It suffers from having been kept offstage for so long that it no longer trusts the microphone. The nothing that comes is not a failure of imagination. It is caution. The private self has watched the public self write with “excellent ideological clarity” and knows exactly how much clarity costs.

This is a problem of tenancy. For three years, your language has belonged to an institutional self. To write for yourself again, you will have to practice a kind of trespassing—using words that are not scored, not cited, not structurally correct. It will feel at first like poor writing, because it will lack the brisk authority of the version of you that knows how to answer to power. That awkwardness is not incompetence. It is the feeling of a muscle lengthening after being held in contraction.

So when you sit for a long time and nothing comes, be gentle with the silence. It is not a block. It is the space between the self who has learned to survive and the self who is trying to remember what it sounds like when survival is not the genre. The writing will return, but it will return as a different kind of writing—smaller, slower, and without the protective architecture you have mastered. You are not losing your ability to write. You are waiting to see if you still believe that your own voice, uncited and unbracketed, is worth the risk of putting on the page.
